When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Desktop projects: Answer/Official from Projects and chats and the multi-folder project release notes. The primary folder supplies new chats' working directory and automatic discovery of AGENTS.md, skills, and config.toml. Secondary folders remain available for searching, reading, and editing; Codex does not automatically discover those project files from secondary folders.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Codex timing: Custom instructions with AGENTS.md describes instruction discovery at startup, once per run, before work begins. It loads global guidance and the instruction files along the path from the project root to the working directory. This establishes startup behavior; it does not promise that a shell cd or an arbitrary file read in another repository triggers instruction injection.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Work timing: The installed desktop app, version 26.1007.30912, has separate primary-folder tooltips for Work and Codex. Both identify the primary folder as the source for AGENTS.md, config.toml, and skills. The strings are in app.asar, at webview/assets/app-initial-6350d04672d0.js, under projectSetup.createLocalProject.primarySourceWorkTooltip and projectSetup.createLocalProject.primarySourceCodexTooltip. This corroborates the primary-folder distinction for Work; the precise event that loads secondary-folder instructions in Work remains unverified.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Context cost: The documented discovery behavior gives no basis for expecting every attached repository's AGENTS.md to enter the initial prompt. Loaded primary-folder guidance still uses context, as do instructions or files subsequently read. This does not establish that attaching folders has zero overhead or quantify usage charges.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

A workable arrangement: Keep shared guidance in a small primary-folder AGENTS.md, with a repository directory map and an instruction to read a target repository's AGENTS.md and applicable nested instructions before working there. Attach related repositories as secondary folders. This asks the agent to load guidance on demand; reliable automatic loading on first access remains an open product question. Starting a separate chat with the target repository as its primary folder gives that repository the documented discovery behavior.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Skills: Build skills documents progressive disclosure for both ChatGPT and Codex: skill names and descriptions are available initially, and the full SKILL.md is read when selected. Skills therefore have a discovery cost even before their full instructions load. Skill activation is based on relevance or explicit invocation, rather than merely changing directories.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Claude comparison: How Claude remembers your project documents startup loading for ancestor CLAUDE.md files and on-demand loading for descendant instructions when a file in that subtree is read, written, or edited. The documented trigger is file use, rather than cd alone. Additional directories supplied with --add-dir have separate memory-loading settings, so nested folders and additional repositories are distinct cases there too.
When does AGENTS.md load in ChatGPT/Work and Codex projects with multiple folders?

Still open as of October 15, 2026: Whether either desktop experience automatically injects a secondary repository's instructions on first access, which tools trigger that behavior, and whether instructions reload after edits. The available documentation supports the primary-folder rule but does not settle those secondary-folder events.

Symptom while trying to add Obsidian Web Clipper: Chrome Web Store showed Switch to Chrome to install extensions and themes, Add to Chrome showed a spinner, then nothing installed.
Is ChatGPT Atlas blocked by the Chrome extension web store when installing extensions like Obsidian Web Clipper? If so, what recourse do users have?
Is ChatGPT Atlas blocked by the Chrome extension web store when installing extensions like Obsidian Web Clipper? If so, what recourse do users have?

Short answer: You are mostly running into compatibility and client-detection limits, not a public “Atlas is banned” announcement. Google Chrome Web Store often refuses or breaks the install flow when the browser is not recognized as Google Chrome, and ChatGPT Atlas (a separate Chromium-based browser from OpenAI) has partial, uneven extension support that can produce exactly the Switch to Chrome banner and failed / stuck installs. Treat Web Clipper on Atlas as unsupported / best-effort until OpenAI documents otherwise.
Is ChatGPT Atlas blocked by the Chrome extension web store when installing extensions like Obsidian Web Clipper? If so, what recourse do users have?

Why the store says “Switch to Chrome”: The Web Store is built around Chrome as the supported install target. Chromium derivatives that do not present the full Chrome identity / capabilities frequently get nudged or blocked at install time. Third-party writeups on Atlas (for example LogRocket’s Atlas overview) call out that message in the context of Atlas not matching Chrome’s extension surface end-to-end. That is store + browser behavior, not proof of a named blocklist against Atlas.
Is ChatGPT Atlas blocked by the Chrome extension web store when installing extensions like Obsidian Web Clipper? If so, what recourse do users have?

What OpenAI has said: The Introducing ChatGPT Atlas post lists safeguards so the agent cannot install extensions for you; that is about automated agent actions, not every manual UI path, but it sits alongside a roadmap that still promises improved developer tools rather than claiming full Chrome parity. Product changes land in ChatGPT / Atlas release notes.

Reality on the ground: Users and extension authors report mixed results—some extensions install or partially work, others fail silently or show odd UI (OpenAI Developer Community — extensions in Atlas). Vendor threads (for example 1Password on Atlas) illustrate work when Atlas + store cooperate, and gaps when deeper integration is missing.

Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows

A terminal-first, standardized, reproducible, dependency-managed dev environment is achievable today without making an IDE your control plane, but there is no single dominant cross-platform standard that literally replaces /bin/zsh with a universal /usr/bin/devcontainersh across all terminals and IDEs.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows
The ecosystem clusters into three practical patterns.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows

The most standardized container-native option for making a container feel like your default shell already exists in Toolbx (toolbox). Its documentation describes toolbox enter as usable as the default shell in a terminal emulation application, and it can create a default container when none exists.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows

If you want per-workspace standardization with the Dev Containers ecosystem (devcontainer.json), the best-aligned primitive is the devcontainer CLI. It provides lifecycle commands like devcontainer up and devcontainer exec, which makes a devcontainersh wrapper straightforward and idempotent.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows

For teams wanting Dev Container compatibility plus local and remote backends and terminal-only usage, DevPod is a prominent approach. It creates environments from devcontainer.json on local Docker or remote machines and clusters, and can be driven from CLI.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows

Outside containers, the most mature terminal-as-environment approach is directory-activated environment management: direnv (and cousins like Shadowenv) with reproducible shells ( Nix/develop, Devbox, devenv, Flox ).
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows
On Linux: Toolbx as a containerized default shell baseline, with optional per-repo Dev Containers via a wrapper when strict per-workspace reproducibility is required.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows
Cross-platform (macOS/Windows/Linux): DevContainer/CLI plus a wrapper script is the closest to per-workspace shell-container semantics aligned to the Dev Containers spec.
Terminal-First Reproducible Dev Environments for Shell-First Workflows
If speed and ergonomics matter more than container isolation: direnv plus a reproducible shell tool (Nix/develop, Devbox, devenv, or Flox).

Autonomous Usage-Quota Discovery for Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Cursor Agent
Autonomous Usage-Quota Discovery for Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Cursor Agent

As of September 15, 2026, there is almost already a single command-line tool for this. The strongest match is aistat, an open-source Go CLI whose explicit purpose is to report and normalize usage limits for Claude/Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub/CoPilot/CLI. It emits JSON by default, has a human-readable mode, reads the credentials already established by the upstream tools, and normalizes provider-specific quotas into common fields such as used_percent, remaining_percent, and resets_at. It is also explicitly designed for usage-aware agent routing.
Autonomous Usage-Quota Discovery for Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Cursor Agent

The missing provider is Cursor. No maintained CLI covers all four. Cursor is the hardest of the four for an individual subscription: current Cursor CLI documentation still does not expose a command for plan/billing quota, and a Cursor staff response specifically says the interactive /usage command reports activity statistics rather than plan spending. Cursor does expose spending and detailed usage APIs for organizational accounts, while individual users are still directed to the Cursor Settings/web usage UI.
Autonomous Usage-Quota Discovery for Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Cursor Agent

Overall recommendation: fork or extend aistat, add a Cursor provider, and gradually replace its private-endpoint adapters with supported local protocols/public APIs where practical. That gets to one agent-friendly executable with the least work.

One important design point: these providers no longer meter in the same unit. Claude and Codex expose rolling usage windows as percentages; current Copilot uses monthly GitHub AI Credits based on model/token cost; Cursor uses model-priced usage pools and billing-cycle spend. A correct abstraction should therefore be "quota windows/resources," not "tokens remaining."

aistat deserves serious consideration before implementing from scratch. Its README describes exactly the orchestration use case: one terminal command that reads Claude, Codex, and Copilot usage, produces normalized machine-readable JSON, and can be consumed by agents to decide where to route work. Its recent releases added multi-account Codex support, model-scoped Claude limits, current Copilot AI-credit support, native Windows support, watching/notifications, and an agent skill.
